1: <!--
2:   ADOPTED 2026-09-22 as the canonical ruleset for A Story of Heroes and Villains.
3: 
4:   This is Ryan's 2026-09-15 consistency pass of V0.6 (see the 2026-09-15 summary in
5:   Planning Docs/Meeting Notes/Design Meeting Summaries.md). It keeps the "V0.6" name but
6:   supersedes, in full:
7:     - Planning Docs/archive/Ruleset-V0.6-2026-09-09.md  (V0.6 as adopted 2026-09-09, migrated
8:                                                          across 0.42.0-0.49.0)
9:     - Planning Docs/archive/Ruleset-V0.5.md and the pre-V0.5 rules files, as that one did.
10: 
11:   The revision's main changes: the universal Hero Roll (final modifier capped at +/-3), Conditions
12:   as Banes rather than -2, a fixed Resist table, the GM's Misfortune currency, the Party as a
13:   character (Party Motif, Party tags, Party Quest, Party Improvements), Connections with Connection
14:   Tags, and a fully rewritten Combat and Enemies chapter (profiles, Guard, Enemy Virtues,
15:   Legendary phases) that finally replaces the V0.5-era Combat Basics text.
16: 
17:   The app does NOT yet implement this revision. Migration is staged in
18:   Planning Docs/WorkPlan-V0.6-Revision.md. Rules questions the revision leaves open are
19:   catalogued in HANDOFF.md under "Known gaps in V0.6"; do not guess at them in code.
20: 
21:   Body below is the document verbatim, unedited, including its three embedded images.
22: -->
23: 
24: # Game Overview
25: 
26: **A Story of Heroes and Villains (ASoHaV) is a narrative-first fantasy game with high-stakes, goal-driven combat.**
27: 
28: This game gives you the tools to craft and tell a story in a world only your table can. You and your fellow players are both author and audience for your favorite High Fantasy movie or television epic. The rules exist to support your story, there is no need to thumb through them to figure out how to take an action; to do it, do it. When you need to roll dice, the sheet in front of you will tell you how the result affects you or the world around you.
29: 
30: Your Heroes will be disparate, complicated people who come together and embark on a journey that will see them change their world in some fundamental way \- big or small. Along their path, they’ll discover their true selves as well as a chosen family they’ll come to defend until the end of days. 
31: 
32: On that path, your Heroes will see fantastic places, meet kind weirdos and cruel monsters; encounter mysteries never before solved; protect the defenseless; they’ll be bold; they’ll take risks; they’ll sing by the fire with friends; they’ll nurture bonds with deep roots; they’ll take down tyrants and trolls alike; they’ll confront the things they’ve always run from (and not wait 30 minutes to swing your sword at a bag of hit points). 
33: 
34: A Story of Heroes and Villains is a game explicitly about Heroes who do all of that. From their first chapter they begin down a path to figuring out the world, themselves, and each other. And should you survive the darkest of evils by relying on those at your side, you’ll have found the place you belong and the people you belong with.
35: 
36: # What is A Story of Heroes and Villains? 
37: 
38: This is a Tabletop Roleplaying game where you and a group of friends tell a story as if you were writing your favorite Epic Fantasy Movie or Television show. You will all take on the responsibilities of crafting the world and the characters within it. Playing the game is largely a conversation, with some structure (the rules) and chaos (the dice) to help drive things forward and create new and interesting situations. 
39: 
40: The great thing about this game is that you are telling this story for and to each other. There’s no better feeling than when something you have all been building toward comes together for the perfect bit of payoff \- either in victory or in tragedy. You all have a pen, you all have a voice. Everyone at the table shares their own ideas that work together to push the story forward. The rules and the dice are here to help guide you \- to surprise you and excite you \- they help set up the next beat of drama for you to explore.
41: 
42: Most of you will be Heroes, directly in control of one of the main characters of your story. One of you will be the Game Master, directly in control of the world around your Heroes. Together, you'll bring your own world to life in a way only your group can. This is your story. Tell it well. Tell it together. Have fun. 
43: 
44: # What Defines This Game?
45: 
46: This game sprung forth from 20 years of playing TTRPGs and consuming Fantasy stories alongside them. In that time we’ve discovered a lot of game mechanics and narrative flavor that really work for our groups and a lot that don’t. What lies before you is the distillation of alllll of that. 
47: 
48: So, is this game for you? Well, are you and your group: 
49: 
50: * Traditional fantasy players who want more character-driven, narrative play.  
51: * Narrative-game players who want more consequential, decision-rich combat.  
52: * Looking for a game that avoids excessive crunch without making danger feel toothless while giving you the tools to tell a meaningful story. 
53: 
54: If you said yes to any one of these (and also you like elves and dragons and magic) then yes\! This is a game for you. Read on. 
55: 
56: **Fiction-First storytelling.**   
57: The rules exist to support the narrative, not the other way around. No mechanical actions happen without the story driving the reason for a rule. You want to Play to Find Out. Nobody at the table knows exactly what is going to happen and when mechanics are triggered, they will never dictate a result of “oh you don’t get through that door, try something else.” They’ll completely change the stakes on everyone at the table\! Maybe you trip a magical alarm or your biggest rival happens to see you fiddling at the lock. The game is never static, the story is always finding new ways to intrigue you both as players and audience members. 
58: 
59: A different way to phrase that is \- “if you say it, do it.” Rather than hunting for what rule can allow you to do something in the game, just do the thing you want to do and the rules will be there to tell you what happens after you do. 
60: 
61: **Fast, high stakes, goal oriented combat.**   
62: Much of what you find in this game could be labeled as being designed within the Powered By the Apocalypse design philosophy. It draws inspiration from the design framework first developed by Vincent Baker for his 2010 game Apocalypse World, and the many, many wonderful games in the PbtA lineage thereafter. However,  there is one big part of this game where we move away from that a bit: Combat. 
63: 
64: The point of “combat” in most narrative heavy games is to function like any other scene in a movie or television show. And as such there is no mechanical distinction between “Role Play” scenes and “Combat” scenes. But the design exploration of what combat can look like has changed drastically since 2010 and we believe this game has found a way to marry Fiction-First, PbtA design with a fully fleshed out, high-stakes combat system that respects your time.
65: 
66: In a game of High Fantasy you’re going to be fighting evil and slaying monsters\! And I think sometimes, in heavy narrative games, it can feel like the tools your Heroes use to navigate social situations are the same ones they use to solve violent ones. In this game, you are making tactical moves in Combat encounters that can dynamically change the stakes of your story. Combat is fast, dangerous, and still finds a way to be easily digestable, while giving back the tactical choices you may miss when playing other narrative-driven games; all without ever wasting your time feeling like you “just have to get through this round” for the good stuff to happen. 
67: 
68: **The game is yours**  
69: And so, before we really get started I want to say, once this book (PDF??) is in your hands, it’s *yours*. Not ours. We’re not in charge of how you have your fun. The whole book is merely our best suggestion of how to have a great, frictionless time telling your Epic Fantasy Story. When in doubt, do what feels most fun. 
70: 
71: # The Setting
72: 
73: The setting is, not to sound like a broken record, High Fantasy. It is built around the idea that the heroes will journey through both dangerous wilds and glorious roads; that they will visit small hamlets in a marsh and enormous port cities on the coast; that they will face down foes in the realm of politics and by way of violence. There will be magic\! There will be monsters\! There will be manipulation\! 
74: 
75: But this text does not contain a codified “setting.” In fact, it is quite the opposite. As part of starting a game of ASoHaV, in addition to creating your characters for your adventuring party, everyone at the table will take part in crafting your unique world. 
76: 
77: # The Players
78: 
79: This game has one player who will be the Game Master (GM) and between two and five players who will be characters. 
80: 
81: For the players portraying characters, it is their responsibility to embody their character’s core conflicts and strengths. They are tasked with bringing the main characters of your tale to life. At all times, you as players should engage with the premise you’ve all agreed to dive into and drive the story forward in the way only your character can. Take risks; protect others; defeat the bad guys. In short \- be heroes\! 
82: 
83: The Game Master is responsible for bringing the world around the main characters to life; to make it feel lived in, dangerous, and wonderous. They play all of your side characters, good and evil, and work together with the players to shine the spotlight in the most interesting places. 
84: 
85: Neither role \- Game Master or character \- is solely responsible for “the story.” In AsoHaV you are all playing to find out what happens next. The GM may set the stage and present interesting opportunities, but that is derived from the histories of all of the characters and the world you set up together. The rules and moves at everyone’s disposal give characters and GMs alike the power to control the narrative at some points and be dragged down the stream of where it takes you at others. Part of the fun is discovering it together\!
86: 
87: In fact, should you ever feel the push to plan what “should” happen next, I implore you not to. There is a real magic to letting the characters and the world find ways to surprise you. The mechanics in this game exist to help you reveal every layer of the proverbial artichoke, and what you’ll find at the end will be like nothing you could have planned for. I don’t want you to cheat yourself out of the butterflies you’ll get when it all comes together as if you planned it, but it is a surprise to everyone at the table. Your characters don’t know where they are headed, so don’t always decide for them. Once you set them and the world up and push over the first domino, it’ll all work out. And soon, before your very eyes, those characters and the world around them will come to life. 
88: 
89: # Getting Started
90: 
91: A Story of Heroes and Villains plays as if you were writing and witnessing your favorite Fantasy movie, TV show, or book. You get to live the most interesting stuff and the boring moments live on the cutting room floor (what interesting means is totally up to your group\!). You do whatever makes sense for your character or, if you’re the GM, the world around the characters, and the mechanics respond to what you do to help you tell a story that is always driving toward interesting moments. 
92: 
93: Of course, as a TTRPG, you’re going to be rolling dice. Always a D6, mostly 2d6 plus a stat, but sometimes 1D6\! However, explicitly, the dice aren’t telling you whether you succeed or fail. They’re telling you what happens next.
94: 
95: ## Live and Play Within the Fiction
96: 
97: The game isn’t structured so that (outside of combat) you’ll say “I use this move.” Instead, you tell or show your group what your character does. If you want to see if there’s a secret passage, don’t ask to make a roll to find out, simply say something like “I start pulling books off the shelf, checking behind the case, looking for anything out of place.” That action might trigger a move. If it does, you roll. If it doesn’t, it just happens. Sometimes the game is an unbroken conversation without a roll. 
98: 
99: A roll only comes into play when there is risk of interesting consequences (positive or negative) at play. If the outcome of something is unclear and/or the stakes matter, you roll. If the outcome is simple or obvious, it just happens. 
100: 
101: The dice come out when things could go wrong or go interesting. 
102: 
103: To put it simply, To do it, you do it.
104: 
105: ## The Dice
106: 
107: When a move triggers, (for example, the Assess the Situation move triggers when you assess the situation to figure out what is going on in a moment of risk or conflict), you roll 2d6 plus one of your character’s Virtue (the move will tell you which). The result on the die sets the stakes for the moment at hand\! We call this the Hero Roll. 
108: 
109: **The Hero Roll**
110: 
111: Whenever a Hero uses a Move, they:
112: 
113: * Roll 2d6 and add the relevant Virtue (usually listed by the Move).   
114: * Add \+1 for *one* relevant Skill Tag and −1 for *every* relevant Flaw Tag.  
115:   * A Hero may push themself once per roll. To **Push Yourself**, mark a Condition and add \+1 for a second relevant Skill Tag.  
116: * The final modifier cannot be beyond \+3 or fall below −3.  
117: * After determining the final modifier, apply Advantage or Disadvantage from Boons, Banes, and other rules.
118: 
119: Results Outside Combat:
120: 
121: * **10+**, You get what you want, sometimes with something extra  
122: * **7–9**, You get what you want, but there’s a cost, complication, or twist  
123: * **6-**, You likely don’t get the outcome you wanted, and something changes \- often for the worse. The GM gains a **Misfortune** and can make a Hard Move immediately if they choose. However, you learn from your failures and mark Potential on one of your Motifs (we’ll explain what that means in a bit). When your party rests, you can trade in 5 Potential from a single Motif when to improve your Hero.
124: 
125: Notice that on a “miss” something is going to change. The story is moving forward no matter what you roll. You never just fail and hit a wall. You won’t roll poorly and get stuck staring at a locked door. When you miss, the situation changes. Maybe a guard spots you or a trap triggers; maybe you DO get what you wanted, but it creates a bigger problem. 
126: 
127: What that is comes out in the conversation between the GM and the other players. 
128: 
129: Results In Combat:
130: 
131: * **10+**, the Hero has maximum impact. Resolve the Move’s greatest normal effect.  
132: * **7–9**, the Hero has moderate impact. Resolve the Move’s standard effect and any brief benefit listed by the Move.  
133: * **6-**, the Hero has limited impact. Resolve the Move’s minimum effect, and the GM gains 1 **Misfortune**.  
134:   * No Potential is gained on a 6- in Combat. 
135: 
136: Combat is a more “zoomed” in look at the fiction. Whereas each role outside of Combat tends to move the fiction a good bit (and you are making less of them per real life minute), rolls in Combat are about a very specific singular moment, each moving the needle a bit less than their out of Combat counterparts. 
137: 
138: ## The Game is a Conversation
139: 
140: You’re going to be talking. To each other. A lot\! The most basic game loop looks like this: 
141: 
142: * The GM describes a situation.  
143: * The characters respond by doing or saying whatever makes sense.  
144: * A move might trigger or something might simply happen.   
145: * The stakes change and the GM continues the conversation by delivering that new information to the characters, either by way of a Non-Player Character (NPC) or by describing the world around them. 
146: 
147: And then it keeps going. Back and forth, over and over. And along the way, really interesting stuff will happen and before you know it you’ll be entrenched in a story that you are all writing and performing for each other. That’s the game\! You can do it\! 
148: 
149: **NOTE: Define “the conversation” as something players can return to to resolve non-rolls.** 
150: 
151: ## Overview of the Gameplay
152: 
153: I’ve mentioned that a session plays like an episode of a show or a chapter in a book. In a session, you can probably expect to participate in one or two big, memorable moments \- maybe a venture through the Whispering Wood or adventuring through the Shadowing Mines; maybe you’re negotiating with nobles or taking down a horde of Trolls. Whatever those may be, they’ll be connected by smaller scenes that connect it all together. Those could be meeting new allies, making camp in a dangerous marsh, or planning your attack on the Keep of Garadale. 
154: 
155: Each moment is driven by character choices. Your Playbooks (the sheet with your character details on it) will have all the juicy drama needed to serve you up the conflict that will lead to these moments. As a Party you’ll also have a big goal. Maybe that goal will be “save the blacksmith’s daughter from the goblins” or “retrieve the Scroll of M’Guffin.” You might resolve a full goal in one session. You might not. Both are right\!.There’s no strict pacing requirement laid out in the rules. The only thing that matters is that you’re doing interesting things to you and your characters.
156: 
157: ### The Adventuring Party
158: 
159: On your Playbook sheet, you’ll see a place for each character’s goals and internal conflicts (DEFINE). In addition, your group shares a larger goal. What that is will change, sometimes often, sometimes infrequently. The individual goals and party goals will first spring forth from character creation. When you make your Heros and adventuring party, you’ll be presented with questions and prompts that build those tensions naturally.
160: 
161: After those goals are out in the open, the GM and other players are free to use that material as it feels natural. You don’t need to force anything \- it will show up in play.
162: 
163: ### The Scenes Make the Story
164: 
165: Think of moments in your game like scenes in a movie. A scene is typically one location or one situation where your characters come into conflict with *something.* The opposing force might be another character or NPC, a societal system, a natural event or creature, or a magical or technological mystery. The conflicting forces can be as small of a scale as a rickety bridge across a river or as large as a final confrontation with the evil necromancer who has been behind all of the party’s woes for months. 
166: 
167: Conflict is what drives the story. Without it, you run the risk of the characters you are portraying saying, “Yeah, so? Why should I care?” And that just takes the air out. 
168: 
169: When you (as a GM or otherwise) are framing a scene to play out, keep in mind what you’d like the central conflict of this moment to be. What is going to stand in the way of the party? And once that conflict has played to its natural conclusion, the scene is over\! You don’t need to play out every single moment. Start late, get out early.  Open the scene at the last possible moment, starting after anything that wouldn’t be enjoyable to play, and ending it as soon as the main point is made. 
170: 
171: Or, to put it simply, skip the boring parts.
172: 
173: ### Framing a Scene? 
174: 
175: Often, it will be the GM who is framing the next scene (though they can ask players to do this as well). They’ll describe what’s happening \- evoking what the characters see, hear, smell, etc; frame the conflict at hand, and then ask: “What do you do?” And then the players act, react. They make decisions. And from those decisions, the stakes of the scene will change and evolve. 
176: 
177: When starting a scene, sometimes the GM will start players in the middle of the action. “You stand hidden at the edge of the forest clearing, the Tomb of the Barrow King, guarded by a pack of six-legged beasts, looms in the misty distance. What do you do?” 
178: 
179: This scene may come after the party decides to travel to the Tomb. If there isn’t inherent risk in playing out the travel, don’t. Maybe you frame it as a passive scene, the GM describing the travel and ending the description as the players “arrive” at the Tomb.
180: 
181: Framing a scene means you’re opening the curtain on something that matters to the Heroes, and then you all deal with it, passing the spotlight between one another to play out the conflict. 
182: 
183: I called out, when starting a new scene, that you want to "start late and leave early." All this means is that a scene should begin as close to the central conflict as possible and end at the exact moment its dramatic purpose is achieved. If you can cut out unnecessary entrances, polite pleasantries, and lingering exits, the table can maintain a tight, engaging pace that respects their own time and your feelings of engagement. The more you do this, the more you can stay focused on what matters \- the vital action and emotional beats that drive your story forward.
184: 
185: In Combat, this is explicitly defined to the table. “You are victorious in this Combat when you save the town crier/retrieve the holy relic.” Outside of Combat, this framing is more implicit. As a GM, it is your job to listen to the characters and the NPCs and, when you see the climax of a scene has happened \- “two characters reach an agreement; an NPC reveals a dramatic secret, an NPC flees the premises” \- it is okay to “cut.” This is really a vibes thing, you’ll get better as you play. When you feel all that needs to happen in a scene has happened, jump to the next, most interesting thing and frame the new situation.
186: 
187: ### The Spotlight
188: 
189: At any given time, the game is focused on someone. That’s the spotlight. It is like the camera is pointing right at them. It might be one of the players or one of the NPCs. The character with the spotlight is taking action \- whatever that means to them. As good collaborators, you want to share the spotlight to highlight your fellow players at the table. Players will often pass the spotlight by having their character ask questions or pose problems to other characters. At any point, the GM can move the spotlight from one character to another by “picking up” the light or camera and “pointing it” at another character, cutting to a new moment or giving a character a chance to respond. 
190: 
191: Keeping the spotlight moving gives everyone a chance to be highlighted and also a chance to support and engage with their fellow player’s choices. What you do when you have the spotlight is up to you. You can describe what your character does or you can speak directly as them. Whatever method, you’re making decisions that will drive your shared story (and may trigger moves\!) forward. 
192: 
193: ### Combat Within Fiction
194: 
195: In ASoHaV, Combat is a different mode of play from everything described before (also known as Freeplay). 
196: 
197: You enter combat when the scene requires violence and that violence has a meaningful outcome, high stakes, or if failing your violent goal would change the story or characters. If a fight feels more like an obstacle, it’s resolved quickly with a Move, Clock, or just played out in the conversation.
198: 
199: At the table you start Combat when you have a goal that requires violence. You’re often not just fighting to “win.” Every combat has a purpose. Perhaps the Parry is rescuing an ally, escaping a treacherous jailer, stealing a precious artifact from a crime lord, or stopping a titan from reaching a defenseless hamlet. Combat isn’t asking the characters to defeat every enemy on the map but rather it is asking them to complete a specific objective. 
200: 
201: #### How Combat Plays
202: 
203: Combat in A Story of Heroes and Villains is played on a map with spaces (either hexagonal or square). You still are driving the fiction forward, but Combat “zooms in” and shows us more of the moment-to-moment minutia. You’re making tactical decisions, considering your position, turn order, and team coordination. But you’re still playing in the fiction. You’re never just saying “I attack.” You’re describing what you do through meaningful choices and moves trigger as a result.
204: 
205: Dice rolls in combat follow the same rules as in Freeplay. There is no pass/fail \- every roll moves you closer or farther from your goal. Good rolls will get you closer to your combat goal and bad roles may progress things only a little, or with negative consequences. No matter what, your turn will change the situation at hand. 
206: 
207: Combat ends when the goal is achieved. If your party has indeed grabbed the artifact, freed the prisoner, or escaped the danger you don’t need to finish the fight by taking out all the remaining bad guys. Once the goal is satisfied, the rest plays out in the conversation. 
208: 
209: You cut to what happens next.
210: 
211: ## Have Fun
212: 
213: And that’s the basics\! You frame a scene, the GM asks the players what they do, everyone acts within the fiction and the mechanics outlined in this text will respond. Then you can watch as conflict sparks and the story changes. There’s no need for some big plan, you’re all working together and will find out what happens together. At the end of each session you’ll end up with what might be your next favorite fantasy epic. 
214: 
215: I also want to stress, if anything in the book doesn’t work for you, or if you find a better way to play \- do that. These mechanics are here to help spark interesting moments. Play the way that works best for you. Don’t get caught up in the specifics. You’re not beholden to me\! I don’t choose what is fun for your group, you do. 
216: 
217: So go have fun. 
218: 
219: # The Game Structure
220: 
221: TALK ABOUT ADVENTURES HERE. TALK ABOUT CAMP. TALK ABOUT PROGRESSION. 
222: 
223: Okay so you’re reading this and I’ve used all of this flowery language to talk about what it “feels” like to play this game. Great. I’ve outlined some of the basics previously. But if you find yourself asking “okay but what does a session look like? What am I actually doing in a session?” Awesome. Check it out.
224: 
225: A Story of Heroes and Villains has two basic modes of play \- Freeplay and Combat. 
226: 
227: You go into Combat when the moment at hand requires violence and the outcome of that violence is meaningful to the players; the stakes are high and failing your Combat goal would change the story or characters in some way. Combat is turn-based and “zooms in” to the moment-to moment action; every little choice moves you closer or farther from your Combat Goal. If a fight feels more like an obstacle, it’s resolved quickly with a single roll or just played out in Freeplay. 
228: 
229: Freeplay is everything that isn’t combat. There is no turn structure. Often, Freeplay begins with the GM describing a situation. Then, the characters respond by doing or saying whatever makes sense. Then, a move might trigger or something might simply happen. After that, the stakes change and the GM continues the conversation by delivering that new information to the characters, either by way of a Non-Player Character (NPC) or by describing the world around them. 
230: 
231: And then it keeps going. Back and forth, over and over. And along the way, really interesting stuff will happen and before you know it you’ll be entrenched in a story that you are all writing and performing for each other. That’s the game\! You can do it\! There are other bits and pieces to help you structure both Combat and Freeplay, but that’s for later in this text.
232: 
233: # Creating the World
234: 
235: The world you play in at your table might be as small as a few towns and their connecting environments or as large as multiple planes navigable only by the stuff of stars. In order to figure out where your story is going to fit on that scale, your group needs to have a conversation to set expectations. Things will run smoothest when everyone is on the same page. And how do you do that? CATS, of course\! 
236: 
237: CATS stands for Concept, Aim, Tone, Subject Matter. It is a concept from the creative mind of Patrick O'Leary. Following the CATS method will allow your group to hit four essential topics quickly and easily. Just start from the top and make your way down.
238: 
239: **Concept**  
240: Discuss the game. At a high-level, what’s it about? In this case, this is a Tabletop Roleplaying game where you and a group of friends tell a story as if you were writing your favorite Epic Fantasy Movie or Television show. You will all take on the responsibilities of crafting the world and the characters within it. Playing the game is largely a conversation, with some structure (the rules) and chaos (the dice) to help drive things forward and create new and interesting situations. 
241: 
242: **Aim**  
243: Explain what the players are trying to accomplish. Are you trying to tell a specific type of story?
244: 
245: * A crew of magical sailors circumnavigating the world in an effort to bring freedom to the oppressed.   
246: * A party of wanna-be-heroes in a city filled with corrupt aristocrats, uncovering secrets and righting wrongs.   
247: * A group of heroes from different walks of life journeying across the kingdom in search of an artifact.   
248: * A team of those who have been hurt by a megalomaniac Dragon, adventuring together to bring it to justice. 
249: 
250: Talk over a few options with your group. What seems fun? What scale are you starting at? Are you aiming for something that lasts five sessions? Ten? Fifty? Get everyone on the same page. 
251: 
252: **Tone**  
253: Talk about what primary attitude, mood, or flavor your game will take on. What is the default? What touchtones are you drawing from? (Serious vs. Silly, Action vs. Drama, etc.). Come to a consensus on what the group wants.
254: 
255: **Subject Matter**  
256: Explain what ideas might be explored during gameplay. Do they make anyone uncomfortable? Discuss what boundaries need to be set, if any.
257: 
258: Afterwards, everyone should have the same expectations for the upcoming game. This discussion shouldn’t be long, but it is essential. 
259: 
260: ## Character Creation
261: 
262: After you’ve done this, go ahead and create your characters. Going through that process will give you a great jumping off point for what your immediate world looks like. You’ll learn a lot of information about what is known (and not known) to the characters and you can start to shape what kind of world they exist in. 
263: 
264: During character and world creation (and honestly, during the main game itself), remember that you are a collaborative team of writers and directors creating an experience together. Don’t worry about keeping secrets from the other players about a hidden backstory. There should be a distinction between player knowledge and character knowledge and you want to use that to your advantage here. 
265: 
266: Make good use of what you know as players and trust that knowing different things from your characters for the sake of dramatic irony will make for engaging storytelling. On the flip side, trust that your characters know more than you do about the world. You, the player, don’t need to know everything. When it makes sense for you to, you will. 
267: 
268: Once you get into the main gameplay loop you’ll find that the more open you can be with your fellow players, the more you can all direct the story in ways that surprise and delight everyone at the table. 
269: 
270: ## Making Your World
271: 
272: Okay, you’ve set expectations, you’ve developed the main characters and their histories with each other. Now it is time to place them in a setting. Throughout character creation, you should have gotten some really juicy ideas about what the world around your characters might be like already. And here’s the fun thing \- you don’t need to know everything right now\! We just need enough to know where we will start in the first session and we’ll sprinkle in some intrigue for future story beats. 
273: 
274: Grab a piece of paper or a shared document, you can do this as a big list, a spreadsheet, or a map you draw together\! Do whatever works for the group. 
275: 
276: This method is adapted from the method found in Lampblack & Brimstone’s *The Perilous Wilds.* 
277: 
278: ## Step 1: Where the Adventure Begins
279: 
280: The first thing you’ll want to do in creating your world is to establish what the general landscape looks like around where your adventure will begin. This can be as simple as deciding “how about we’re in some sort of, like, village in between two mountain ranges?” or “what if the characters all start on a small island.” 
281: 
282: Whatever it is, once everyone is in agreement, everyone introduces one detail about the local area and jots it down (or sketches it on the map). Something like a mysterious lighthouse, a thick forest, an old ruin, or a large lake. 
283: 
284: Now, decide on a name for this place. If it is a town, you might call it something like Kaimora, Hillshire, or Red Sun City; if it is an old tomb in a dark wood you might call it something like The Tomb of the Barrow King or simply The Forgotten Mausoleum. 
285: 
286: Next, starting with whoever has an idea first, take turns answering the following questions: 
287: 
288: * This place is famous for:   
289: * It is infamous for:   
290: * When it comes to resources (natural or economic), this place is  
291:   * Prospering, floundering, etc.   
292: * Because of the resource situation one thing that is happening here is:   
293: * A notable organization or group that is known to call this place home is:   
294: * The nearest neighboring town is:   
295: * That town’s relationship with this place is  
296:   * Amicable, competitive, envious, charitable, etc. 
297: 
298: Each player then shares one rumor about the place where the party will start. The rumor can be anything\! A bit of everyday drama or something supernatural. It could be a small secret or something everyone here has heard of. 
299: 
300: You’ll jot these down and the GM will use the details of character and world creation to help shape the story as you play. These rumors might appear in strange and twisted ways as the narrative moves forward, and some of them may not come up at all \- but getting them all out there will give you all a great foundation to start your adventure. 
301: 
302: ## Step 2: The Surrounding Regions
303: 
304: You know where you’re starting and some top-level details about what that place is. Now let’s zoom out just a bit and put that region in context of the world around it. 
305: 
306: Starting with anyone who wants to speak and then rotating clockwise (including the GM), everyone is going to add a region to the map. A region is just a big section of land or water. You can define what the terrain looks like (a misty forest, rocky plateau, stormy badlands, etc) or by who occupies it (an imperial kingdom, disparate nomads, wild creatures, etc). 
307: 
308: When it’s your turn, say which category of region you are adding (terrain type or political occupant) and then jot that info down. Feel free to give one interesting truth or rumor about that region, but don’t feel pressure to. After that, give the region a name. If you can’t think of a name? Just roll on the table below\! 
309: 
310: The first region should overlap with your starting place. After that, the region you create on your turn can be close or far from your starting region. This part of collaborative world building will codify your starting scale. Are we looking at the coast of one country or kingdom? The entirety of the seas? Or perhaps the magical links between entire realms? 
311: 
312: Whatever type of region you choose, I’d suggest creating something different from the person before you \- the more variety the better. It shouldn’t be a land of *only* witchy forests (unless…). 
313: 
314: Once everyone has gone once, decide if you have enough or if everyone should go again. 
315: 
316: TABLE\! Combine a bunch of region generating tables. Probably should do a town/city one too. The Perilous Wilds is a good starting point. 
317: 
318: ## Step 2: Places of Interset
319: 
320: Now, starting with the player whose character is the most traveled, and continuing clockwise, each player adds either an area, a settlement, or a landmark. These are specific places of interest, near or far, you’ll find in the various regions (including your starting region) that may affect the story or your party may visit. Keep making Places of Interest until you feel satisfied (maybe somewhere around eight?). 
321: 
322: The three categories for Places of Interest are: 
323: 
324: * **Areas:** These are smaller zones inside a region. Think of them like a "mini-region” with something intriguing about it, like a single barren patch in a huge forest or a small island in the middle of the sea. Jot or mark that down. It can span or straddle multiple regions if that makes sense.   
325: * **Settlements:** These are basically anywhere people live, like a little hamlet, a castle, or a big city. Give it a name and pick where it goes. If you’re drawing a blank on a name, see the table below.  
326: * **Landmarks:** These can be almost anything where something interesting is happening, mundane or magical. It could be anything from an odd formation in the landscape, to a wizard’s tower, to a wandering torrent of darkness that roams the land. Name it and place it somewhere in a region. 
327: 
328: ## Step 3: Personal Places
329: 
330: Now, starting with the eldest character, everyone (except the GM) is going to give a specific location \- either a place they call home or a place that holds some significance to them. This place can be somewhere you’ve already established or it can be a brand new Place of Interest. Name it and add it to your world\! Again, if you need help naming, use the tables below. 
331: 
332: For this personal place of significance, name one event that happened there that was important to your character. Something that shaped who they are today. A celebration, a tragedy, or maybe their catalyst for adventure. If you need help on this, refer to the questions you answered during character creation. 
333: 
334: ## Step 4: Create Connectors
335: 
336: Now start with a player who hasn’t gone first yet and keep rotating clockwise. This time, you’ll be adding important connectors to your world. A connector is anything that helps people or things from A to B. That could be a road, a river, a secret path, interplanar portals, or an arcane ley line. These connectors can stretch between different regions and can even head off into parts unknown. 
337: 
338: When it’s your turn, decide where the path goes and give it a name. Remember water flows from high ground to something bigger like a lake or ocean (unless it is magical\!) and settlements of people can usually be found near water. 
339: 
340: Add connectors until you have five or so marked. All of these things you’ve added are not a finite list, you can add more of any of them as your adventure plays out. 
341: 
342: ## Step 5: Start Rumors
343: 
344: Starting with whatever character has the highest Guile, each player (except the GM) says a rumor their character has heard about any place on the map. It might be true, it might be false, but they’ve heard it said somewhere. The rumor should be interesting enough that heroes or villains might seek it out. The other players at the table can ask any clarifying questions if needed. 
345: 
346: # Heroes
347: 
348: # Hero & Party Creation
349: 
350: # Who are you?
351: 
352: Choose your: **Name, Pronouns, and Physical Description.** What do people see when they look at your character? 
353: 
354: # Hero Motifs
355: 
356: **Hero Motifs** are the core aspects of your Hero. They help define their background, skills, and experiences thus far in their life.
357: 
358: Choose Three Motifs (repeat picks allowed) and write them at the top of each of your Motif Slots. You may change the name of any of the Motifs to better match your character’s flavor. If some or none of the Motifs feel right for you, create one or more of your own.  Your Motifs will act as buckets for associated Skills, Flaws, and Quests. 
359: 
360: **Artisan**: You are skilled in a grounded craft or lifelong trade, honed through quiet dedication and practice
361: 
362: **Bearer**: You carry a relic of profound power, it has a legacy of magic, mystery, or myth.
363: 
364: **Devoted**: You have an unshakable loyalty to a cause, creed, or companion.
365: 
366: **Exalted/Lowly**: Your rank, reputation, and influence within the intricate webs of society.
367: 
368: **Exemplar**: You have a defining temperament or worldview. Or perhaps some specific physical, mental, or emotional qualities.
369: 
370: **Fated**: You walk a prophesied path, divine calling, or inexorable fate.
371: 
372: **Forged**: You have been defined by some crucible of your past; a defining trauma, triumph, or event that shaped you.
373: 
374: **Inheritor**: You are greatly affected by the bloodline, culture, and traditions of the people you call your own.
375: 
376: **Mystic**: You wield an ability with the unseen or supernatural forces that shape the world.
377: 
378: **Mythic**: You are a creature of magic or myth.
379: 
380: **Sage**: You carry rare or secret knowledge. Perhaps due to arcane or divine insight, or specialized schooling.
381: 
382: **Sworn**: You’ve sworn a solemn oath, sacred mission, or heavy mantle.
383: 
384: **Virtuoso**: You display a breathtaking raw talent, hard-won skill, or impressive mastery.
385: 
386: ## Skill Tags
387: 
388: Skill Tags mechanically express the experiences and proficiencies your character has gained up to this point (you’ll gain more Skill Tags as you adventure). A Skill Tag can give \+1 to any relevant roll. There is no defined list of skills, they are simply words or phrases that say something true and have an effect on how you interact with the world. 
389: 
390: Under each Motif, write one Skill Tag. Below are some suggestions to use. You aren’t confined to using them as they are listed (or at all). If the Skill Tag “Alchemist’s Satchel” feels better for you under “Artisan” than “Bearer,” do that. You can also create any Skill Tag yourself to go under your Motif that you and your GM agree on. 
391: 
392: During the game, when one of your Skill Tags applies to any roll you are about to make, you can use that tag to demonstrate your proficiency. Before rolling you can declare your Skill Tag to add its \+1 to the roll. If more than one of your skills applies, you may **Push Yourself.**  Mark one **Condition** and add an additional \+1 to your roll.  
393: 
394: ### Skill Tag Examples
395: 
396: **Artisan**
397: 
398: Armorer, Artificer, Baker, Blacksmith, Bowyer and Fletcher, Brewer of Potent Spirits, Camp Cook, Carpenter, Cunning Trapmaker, Field Medic, Inventor, Jeweler, Leatherworker, Locksmith, Meticulous Mapmaker, Ol’ Stablemaster, Reliable Wagonwright, Ropemaker and Rigger, Seasoned Shipwright, Stonemason, Tailor, Tinker, Traveling Apothecary, Undertaker’s Trade
399:

  Body below is the document verbatim, unedited, including its three embedded images.
